title: Plasma Hydrodynamics Enhance Filtered Pseudoscalar Dark Matter Abundance
excerpt: Physicists have shown that plasma hydrodynamics can significantly boost the abundance of pseudoscalar dark matter during first-order cosmological phase transitions.
content:
Theoretical physicists have modeled how plasma hydrodynamics significantly alters the predicted relic abundance of pseudoscalar dark matter produced during a cosmological first-order phase transition.

As the assumed mass of the dark matter particle increases, the research team identified three distinct patterns of evolution prior to nucleation, ranging from complete thermal equilibrium to thermal suppression and eventual freeze-out.

For a wall velocity parameter of ξw = 0.01, numerical simulations demonstrated that hydrodynamic effects boost the final dark matter abundance Yχ by factors of approximately 4.1, 5.7, and 31.6 for dark matter masses of 1.78 TeV, 2.30 TeV, and 5.03 TeV, respectively. These calculations indicate that heavier dark matter particles experience substantially larger relative enhancements due to plasma interactions during the transition.

For the two lighter particle mass benchmarks of 1.78 TeV and 2.30 TeV, the numerical and analytic predictions agreed within 5 percent when hydrodynamic effects were excluded. When hydrodynamic influences were incorporated into the calculations, the discrepancy between numerical and analytic solutions decreased further to approximately 1 percent or less.

In contrast, the heaviest examined case of 5.03 TeV required a dedicated numerical treatment because dark matter freeze-out occurs prior to bubble nucleation. The numerical modeling established that hydrodynamic reheating can boost the final yield even in regimes where dark matter particles have already decoupled from the plasma prior to the onset of the phase transition.

Under conditions where pre-nucleation freeze-out takes place, the final dark matter abundance is determined jointly by the pre-existing abundance set before nucleation and the subsequent hydrodynamic filtering occurring directly at the bubble wall.
